visits.text: Mont Orgueil makes you work for it: nearly 200 steps lead to the top, above Gorey’s harbor. Begun in 1204 after the loss of Normandy, the castle conceals a medieval “urine wheel” and, paradoxically, German rangefinding posts disguised as old stonework. In winter, visit from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., with last admission at 3 p.m.

The detour is worth it: La Pouquelaye de Faldouet, a dolmen with a passage dating back around 6,000 years, opens into a double chamber with a 24-tonne capstone over the rear section. Admission is free year-round, in a meadow near Gorey. Wear high-top shoes if the grass is wet.

activities.text: Head down for a stroll around Gorey’s harbor in the late afternoon, when the low sunlight turns Mont Orgueil’s ramparts golden. In the early 19th century, at least 2,000 men here made their living from oysters, and a group of sculptures commemorates the village’s shipyards. The harbor basin dries out at low tide: for reflections, aim for high tide.

visits.text: A castle that barely saw service: Grosnez Castle, begun around 1369, was captured by Du Guesclin as early as 1373 and dismantled. Its main surviving feature is the gateway arch, 60 meters above the sea, facing the other Channel Islands. Admission is free; at night, this headland is among the island’s best spots for stargazing.

activities.text: If the sea has receded, head down to Plémont Bay: low tide reveals sea caves, natural pools with sandy bottoms, and a freshwater waterfall. At high tide, the sand disappears, leaving only rocks. Time your visit for low tide and head back up as soon as the tide starts coming in.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: La Corbière occupies Jersey’s southwestern tip, and La Corbière Lighthouse, first lit in 1874, was the first in the British Isles built of concrete. A causeway leads to it at low tide; a plaque commemorates assistant keeper Peter Larbalestier, who drowned in 1946 while trying to save a visitor. When the alarm sounds, the tide is rising: return to shore immediately.

activities.text: Wilder than the southern coves, St Ouen’s Bay stretches along eight kilometers of Atlantic-facing sand: it is Jersey’s longest beach. Its surfers have one of Europe’s oldest clubs, and dunes spread out just across the road. Stop on your way down to La Corbière for a walk with your feet in the sea foam.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: Cool stone and dim light: the passage at La Hougue Bie extends some 20 meters beneath a 12-meter-high mound. This Neolithic tomb dates from around 4000 to 3500 BC and has two medieval chapels on top. At the equinoxes, the rising sun reaches the back of the chamber; the site is open year-round.

Unearthed in Grouville in 2012, the Câtillon II hoard—around 70,000 coins and pieces of jewelry buried some 2,000 years ago—is considered the world’s largest Celtic hoard. Beneath the mound at La Hougue Bie, a German command bunker tells the story of the Organisation Todt’s forced laborers. Allow 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: St Aubin served as the trading capital before St Helier: until around 1840, St Helier had only a small quay, and trade passed through here. Cod from Gaspé paid for many houses on Rue du Crocquet, and the Old Court House is said to have housed the privateers’ prize court. Follow the Jersey Heritage walking tour, which takes about 45 minutes.

activities.text: Watch for low tide to walk out to St Aubin’s Fort, perched on its islet in front of the harbor. Its 16th-century tower, reinforced during the English Civil War and later fitted with bunkers by the Germans, protected ships at anchor. Set off from in front of the Royal Channel Islands Yacht Club and keep an eye on the time: the tide comes in quickly.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: According to legend, the p’tits faîtchieaux moved the building site of St Brelade’s Church to the shore every night: the church has remained beside the bay. Next door, the Fishermen’s Chapel preserves an Annunciation painted around 1310–1315, and its name may derive from “pécheurs” (sinners) rather than “pêcheurs” (fishermen). Look for limpet shells in the walls.

activities.text: Spread your towel on the golden sand of St Brelade’s Bay, popular for its sheltered swimming and water sports. The Sir Winston Churchill Memorial Park is also in the bay. Save this break for late afternoon, just after visiting the church, and check the tide times.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: At low tide, walk to Elizabeth Castle along the roughly 1.1 km causeway: allow at least 15 minutes and watch for the incoming tide. Otherwise, the amphibious Castle Ferry departs from West Park. Begun in 1594, the fort was named after Elizabeth I by Walter Raleigh, and Charles II took refuge here in 1649. Continue to the Hermitage, the rock where Saint Helier is said to have lived around 550. Open from late March to late October.

Step inside the Maritime Museum on New North Quay to understand how the sea shapes life on Jersey, where the largest tides can reach twelve meters. In the same complex, the Occupation Tapestry Gallery displays thirteen panels woven by residents of the twelve parishes for the fiftieth anniversary of the Liberation. An exhibition also traces the fates of the ten islanders who sailed on the Titanic as passengers and crew. The display panels have captions in English and French; the site is open year-round.

Lit by gaslight, the Victorian house at Jersey Museum depicts a family in crisis: that of Dr. Charles Ginestet, who eventually left for France. Upstairs, the La Tèrr’rie d’Jèrri exhibition tells the island’s story through its objects, while a portrait of Lillie Langtry by Millais catches the eye. Admission to the ground floor, with its film and Geopark visitor center, is free: use it to plan your coastal walks before buying a ticket for the full museum.

Islanders called it the Vier Marchi: Royal Square hosted the town market until 1806. On January 6, 1781, most of the Battle of Jersey was fought here in 15 minutes; Baron de Rullecourt died of his wounds in the house that became The Peirson pub, named after the young major killed that day. Look up at the gilded statue of George II, unveiled in 1751, in front of the Royal Court.

activities.text: Ornate cast iron, fruit stalls, and a three-tiered fountain flowing at its center: built in 1882, the Central Market boasts the island’s finest cast-iron architecture, according to Jersey Heritage. Look for the animal, fruit, and vegetable motifs at the entrances, then cross Beresford Street to the fish market, built in 1841. Visit in the morning for the lively atmosphere and pick up supplies for the next day’s picnic.

visits.text: Excavated between 1941 and 1945 by the Organisation Todt, which used forced laborers, the Jersey War Tunnels comprise more than a kilometer of underground passages. They were intended to become a 500-bed hospital, which was never used before the German surrender in May 1945. The temperature stays around 17 °C year-round: bring a sweater and enter before the last admission at 4 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Jersey in 3 Days: Castles, Tides, and Durrell’s Zoo

visits.text: Start your visit to Jersey Zoo with the gorillas. N’Pongo, who arrived in 1959, was thought to be male, so a female companion was purchased for her. In 1986, the silverback Jambo protected a child who had fallen into the enclosure. Gerald Durrell’s 13-hectare zoo breeds endangered species. Arrive at 9:30 a.m. with a dated ticket booked online for 10% less.
